RECOVERABLE, PROBABLY — but the specific method we named is the wrong one, and the causal framing is open while the decision-theoretic framing is fully occupied.

THE ONE NUMBER, from the only paper with sub-8B models on our exact benchmarks with hidden-test grading (DOCE, arXiv:2408.13745, n=50): execution-agreement selection applied AFTER the visible-test filter recovers 63.0-76.6% of the filter-to-oracle gap on HumanEval+ and MBPP-S+ for CodeLlama-7B-Instruct and DeepSeekCoder-6.7B-Instruct (MEASURED rows; gap fractions INFERRED). Closest cell to us, DeepSeekCoder-6.7B on MBPP-S+: Filter 72.6 -> Filter+MBR-Exec 82.1, Oracle 85.6, i.e. 73.1%. Mapped onto our 3B (filter 0.7455, oracle 0.8192, gap 0.0737) that projects +0.046 to +0.057 absolute, landing at 0.792-0.803; on our 7B (gap 0.0351), +0.022 to +0.027. Both are an order of magnitude above the zero our GBM and logistic static-feature models returned, and the same DOCE table independently reproduces our null: log-likelihood selection on top of the filter adds only +0.7/+0.4/+0.7/-1.1 pp, i.e. 3-5% of the gap.

THE CORRECTION TO OUR PLAN, and it is the highest-value finding here: "run every candidate on common inputs and prefer the largest output-agreement cluster" is NOT untested. It is AlphaCode-C, benchmarked in CodeT (arXiv:2207.10397, ICLR 2023). At n=100 on the sub-8B InCoder-6B it is worth +1.3pp on HumanEval and +5.4pp on MBPP, and it is NEGATIVE on 2 of 4 model-benchmark cells (CodeGen-16B: -2.4 and -1.4). CodeT diagnoses why: raw cluster size is captured by trivial wrong solutions that agree because they all crash or all return None. Everything that WORKS in the literature adds one of two things on top: the visible-test filter first (DOCE: 49.5 -> 70.1 on CodeLlama-7B HumanEval+, the filter is doing most of the work) or generated tests with expected outputs (CodeT: 26.7 -> 34.4 over clustering on InCoder-6B MBPP). So the arm to run is FILTER-THEN-AGREEMENT, not agreement.

WHERE THE EVIDENCE DOES NOT EXIST, stated plainly because the absence is itself our result: NOT ONE paper reports execution-agreement selection at k<=8 for a sub-8B model. DOCE sweeps n=5..50 but has NO table at n=5 or n=10 — only figure curves, and its own prose says the method "scal[es] much better with more candidates", so we would be sitting on the rising part of the curve. CodeT's small-number ablation is over TEST CASES (10/20/50/100), not candidates; candidates are fixed at n=100. Semantic Voting (arXiv:2605.08680, May 2026) uses N=50/100 and three Gemini preview endpoints with undisclosed parameter counts whose WEAKEST configuration greedy-decodes 76.2% on HumanEval+ and 91.3% on MBPP+ — stronger than our 3B's 0.7169. The only genuine k=8 result in the whole set (OSCA, NAACL 2025: 67% on LiveCodeBench at 8 samples, beating default allocation at 128 samples, a 128x compute multiple) is on 70B-and-up models and allocates across configurations, a lever we do not have. Our regime is unoccupied territory, and that is both the opportunity and the reason the 63-77% figure is an UPPER BOUND, not a forecast.

TWO MEASURED DISCOUNTS ON THAT UPPER BOUND. (1) Information: DOCE's MBR-Exec "use[s] all unit tests given but only their inputs" — it executes on EVALUATION test inputs, which our strict visible/hidden split forbids. DOCE itself calls this "impractical". We must self-generate inputs, and Semantic Voting measures what that costs: input quality is the single largest factor, with sketch-based generation beating random fuzzing by up to 11.3 pp — large enough to eat most of our projected 4.6-5.7 pp. (2) Diversity: agreement needs distinct execution fingerprints, and a single quantized 3B at fixed temperature is the worst case for producing them. THIS IS FREE TO CHECK RIGHT NOW: count distinct execution fingerprints per task in the existing 3-4-draw logs. If most tasks yield fewer than 3, clustering cannot reach 0.0737 and the 20,000-call experiment should not be run. Zero receiver calls, and it is the correct gate before spending 22 contended hours.

ON OUR REGIME BEING VIABLE AT ALL: the one paper in our actual band (Feedback Over Form, arXiv:2604.21950, April 2026 — Gemma3:1B, Qwen2.5:1.5B, Llama3.2:3B, Qwen2.5-coder:3B on HumanEval and MBPP-sanitized) explains our residual gap mechanistically: SyntaxError fix rate 100%, NameError 50-67%, AssertionError only 4-24%. At 3B the surviving failures are LOGIC errors, which is exactly why cheap static features recovered nothing. It also corroborates our stopping result directly — without early stopping "every iteration is net-negative", -6 to -22 net NEW failures per iteration — which is independent external support for our paired -0.0182 [-0.0260, -0.0105]. And it issues a warning we should act on: their single-run results were inflated 5-7% versus 5-run means, which matters because our 7B gap is only 0.0351 and may not survive replication.

IS THE CAUSAL / DTR FRAMING OCCUPIED? NO — and the gap is unusually clean. Selection-and-stopping for LLM inference has been framed four separate ways, none of them causal: optimal stopping / Pandora's Box with Weitzman + UCB (arXiv:2510.01394, Oct 2025, 15-35% fewer generations at matched quality, on AlpacaFarm/HH-RLHF with reward-model scores); Bayesian optimal stopping for self-consistency (arXiv:2602.05395, ICML 2026, up to 50% fewer calls, with a transferable "L=3 is all you need" theorem); constrained policy optimization with a cheap-feature classifier (arXiv:2604.14853, Apr 2026, Qwen2.5-7B included, up to 12.8% relative on MATH, >91% oracle imitation); and predicted-marginal-reward adaptive best-of-k (arXiv:2410.04707, 50% compute cut or 10% quality gain). I verified explicitly that NONE of them uses propensities, randomized assignment, or an identification argument. Meanwhile the exact inference theory our design needs was published in stat.ME in February 2026 with zero LLM contact — arXiv:2602.15559, martingale AIPW/DML with LOGGED PROPENSITIES, giving fixed-horizon Studentized N(0,1) inference with variance from realized quadratic variation under sequential randomization and predictably-fit nuisances, all conditions we satisfy by construction. The two halves have not been joined.

THE NEAREST NEIGHBOUR, and it rules itself out for us: arXiv:2605.01311 (Jin & Syrgkanis, Stanford, May 2026) does put LM generation in a do-calculus frame — mu(a)=E[Y(do(A=a))], identified from a small randomized experiment plus a simulator, with SWE-bench Verified programmatic outcomes on 500 issues. But its treatment is MODEL CHOICE, not which candidate to return or when to stop; it is not propensity-based; and its Assumption A4 explicitly confines it to "single-round, stateless generation", stating that in "repeated, adaptive, or multi-round interactions... A4 fails." It names our territory and declines to enter it. Its existence does cost us one claim: programmatic outcomes as the reward in causal LM evaluation is no longer novel.

VERDICT ON OUR SURVIVING CLAIM: OPEN on the causal/DTR axis, ADJACENT-AND-CROWDED on the algorithmic axis. Defensible novelty = prospective randomization with known logging propensities + identified sequential selection-and-stopping + programmatic hidden-test outcome + the k<=8, sub-8B, quantized regime nobody reports. NOT novel = adaptive best-of-N (Damani et al. 2024), execution-agreement selection (Shi et al. EMNLP 2022 / CodeT ICLR 2023 / DOCE 2024 / Semantic Voting 2026), stopping rules (2510.01394, ICML 2026), programmatic causal outcomes (2605.01311). One structural warning from the MRT literature we borrow the design from (Klasnja et al. 2015; arXiv:1711.03587): MRTs are powered on hundreds-to-thousands of randomization occasions per unit and we have 8, so essentially all our power is cross-task, not within-task — any claim about how the effect varies across draw index 1 through 8 will be badly underpowered, and sequential IPW variance compounds, so use the AIPW/DML form, not plain importance weights. Also prespecify band-stratified reporting: the one multi-turn LLM OPE paper that exists (arXiv:2510.17173, NeurIPS 2025 workshop, 7 users / 280 turns, no propensities) found an average gain that masked subgroup harm.

RECOMMENDED SEQUENCE, budget-reconciled at 909 calls/hour: (0) fingerprint-diversity audit on existing logs, 0 calls, hard gate; (1) if it passes, 8 draws x 561 tasks = 4,488 calls ~ 4.9 hours, arms = filter-only (our 0.7455 baseline), filter-then-agreement, agreement-alone as the AlphaCode-C replication we now know will likely lose; (2) input generation is the binding constraint, not draws — derive inputs from the single visible assertion plus cheap mutation before spending receiver calls on sketch generation; (3) the 20,000-call / 22-hour design is not justified until step 0 and step 1 return. Target to beat: filter-only 0.7455, with the literature-implied ceiling at 0.792-0.803 and CodeT's AlphaCode-C evidence saying a naive version may land at or below 0.7455.

HEADLINE, in the form requested. Symbolic/execution agreement clustering closes 54.7% of the pass@1-to-oracle gap at k=5 and 60.2% at k=10 on HumanEval+ for open models of 4B-20B (SEP, arXiv:2604.06485; INFERRED from their Tables 1 and 3; mean gap 0.098 at N=5 and 0.119 at N=10). Generated-test agreement (CodeT) closes 31.2% at k=5 and 32.4% at k=10 in the same tables. On the three sub-5B cells alone at k=5 the numbers are CodeT 30.5% and SEP 53.0% of a 0.0993 gap. On frontier models at k=50 the gap is essentially gone: residual selection failures average only 1.5-2.7% and one configuration hits exactly 0.0% (Semantic Voting, arXiv:2605.08680, MEASURED-IN-PAPER).  SO THE ANSWER IS: YES, THE GAP IS RECOVERABLE -- BUT NOT FROM THE BASELINE WE ACTUALLY HAVE. Every one of those percentages is measured against raw single-sample pass@1, not against a visible-test-filtering baseline. Our visible-assertion rule already closes 28.0% of our 3B gap (INFERRED: (0.7455-0.7169)/(0.8192-0.7169)), which is the entirety of what CodeT-strength agreement delivers. The only two papers that measure agreement ON TOP OF visible-test filtering, at our k, on our model scale, both report nothing: S* (EMNLP Findings 2025, Table 3, N=8, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct) gives public-tests-only 42.3, generated-test agreement 42.3 (+0.0 pp), LLM-judge 42.3 (+0.0 pp), and only pairwise adaptive input synthesis 44.5 (+2.2 pp) -- with a four-model average for generated-test agreement of -0.7 pp, i.e. NEGATIVE; and arXiv:2606.16999 (k=8, frozen 0.5B-1.5B code models, MBPP+/HumanEval+) reports every execution-consensus operator null, with residual hidden-correctness AUC 0.479 among visible-passing candidates on Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B, realized consensus gains of 0-2 tasks at p >= 0.25, and a selector-agnostic ceiling of 0 tasks on its DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B cell.  THE LITERATURE SPLITS EXACTLY ON THE AXIS WE CARE ABOUT, AND THAT IS THE DECISION. Above 4B, measured against pass@1, at k>=5: agreement recovers half the gap. At or below 1.5B, or measured against visible-test filtering at k=8: it recovers zero. Our receivers (3B and 7B, q4_k_m) sit in the unmeasured band between those two findings, and our baseline is the visible-test one. Nobody has run this cell. That is the whole of our remaining scientific room, and it is genuinely open -- but it is one experiment wide, not a paper wide.  WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE DECISION, IN NUMBERS. (1) Run agreement clustering on the 3B first, never the 7B. The 3B residual gap above the visible rule is 0.0737; the 7B is 0.0351, which over 448 tasks is about 15.7 flippable tasks (INFERRED) -- McNemar-significant only if harm is near zero, so a 50% recovery with 5 regressions lands at p around 0.5. The 7B arm cannot carry a result. (2) Cost it before running it: H2's SEP needs bounded symbolic execution (CPU only, no receiver calls, 539s per benchmark at N=5) while H4's +2.2 pp needs pairwise LLM input synthesis, which in that paper was done by GPT-4o-mini and not by the small receiver -- at 909 calls/hour, pairwise synthesis over 8 candidates on 230 tasks is thousands of calls and roughly a contended day. Prefer the symbolic/CPU route; it is the only version of this that fits a shared M5. (3) Pre-test for free. H7 (COLM 2024) released 1,328,000 Code Llama 7B generations for HumanEval and MBPP; subsample to k=8 and measure agreement-vs-visible-filter gap closure at zero receiver cost before committing any of the 22-hour budget. (4) Report the false-positive rate of our own visible-assertion selector against hidden tests. H5 shows false positives scale inversely with single-sample accuracy on exactly HumanEval and MBPP, and worst for the weakest models, so an unaudited 0.8192 oracle is a contestable number and part of the 0.0737 may be unrecoverable by construction.  AND THE HONEST VERDICT ON THE PAPER AS FRAMED. It does not survive. "Selection and stopping under known propensities, validated against adaptive best-of-N" is occupied on all four sides: H1 already published the null for post-hoc selection operators at k=8 on small local code models with a stronger protocol than ours (26 operators, do-no-harm McNemar bar, leakage and determinism gates) AND a certified stopping rule (ACE, ~19% compute cut at zero harm, p=0.0165); H6 already owns stopping as optimal-stopping theory (15-35% fewer generations); H3 already showed the aggregation RULE is statistically irrelevant (p>0.05 in 18/18 configurations, SV-minus-WV in [-0.79,+0.61] pp) so any contribution framed as a better agreement or stopping rule is pre-refuted, with input quality the only live variable; and H7 already published our static-feature null in 2024. What is left that nobody has done is narrow and specific: the causal/randomized ESTIMATION layer -- prospective randomization with known propensities and paired confidence intervals on the selection and stopping decisions, in the 3B-7B quantized band, against an adaptive best-of-N baseline, at k<=8. Our measured -0.0182 [-0.0260, -0.0105] for adaptive best-of-N beating a real feedback loop is the one number in this project that no paper found here reports, because none of them randomize and none of them give paired intervals. That is a methods contribution, not a selection-method contribution, and it should be pitched that way or not at all.

RECOVERABLE, but by execution agreement plus synthesised inputs, not by any learned selector we can afford -- and the honest expected size is +0.02 to +0.03, not the +0.05 to +0.06 the headline literature implies. (1) The single closest paper, DOCE (arXiv:2408.13745), runs our exact design on our exact benchmarks at our model scale: DeepSeekCoder-6.7B-Instruct, HumanEval+/MBPP-S+ under EvalPlus hidden tests, visible-("trial")-test filtering as the baseline. Adding MBR-Exec output-agreement clustering on top of filtering moves 78.7 -> 90.7 with oracle 93.2 on HumanEval+ and 72.6 -> 82.1 with oracle 85.6 on MBPP-S+, i.e. agreement clustering closes 82.8% and 73.1% of the post-filter oracle gap at k=50 on a 6.7B model (numbers MEASURED-IN-PAPER, fractions INFERRED). (2) The same table is the strongest published corroboration of our null: execution-FREE rerankers stacked on the same filter add +0.4/+0.2 (log-likelihood) and +0.9/+0.2 (Coder-Reviewer), i.e. 1.5-6.2% of the gap, and the TRAINED execution-free metric CodeScore scores 63.6 against Random 65.1 and degrades filtering (78.4 vs 78.7) -- "does not even outperform the random baseline". CodeRM (arXiv:2501.01054, ACL 2025) independently shows a trained scalar reward model at -0.80 on MBPP+ with Llama3-8B and -2.59 with GPT-4o-mini; AceCoder (arXiv:2502.01718, ACL 2025) shows its in-distribution-trained RM at -0.6 below greedy on HumanEval with Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, one of our own receiver families; Scaling Agentic Verifier (arXiv:2602.04254) shows a grading RM at -0.9 below vanilla at Best@64. Our four null fractions (-0.18, -0.06, 0.00, 0.00) are a replication, not a pipeline bug. (3) THE EVIDENCE GAP THAT DECIDES OUR DESIGN, stated explicitly because it is decision-relevant: essentially the entire execution-agreement literature is run at k=25 to k=1000 on models at or above 6.7B, unquantized. CodeT (k=100), LEVER (k=100), CodeRM (N=100), MPSC (200 solutions + 500 tests), ACES (~200 candidates), Weaver (K=100), Semantic Voting (N=50), Coder-Reviewer (k=25). CodeT -- the field's most-cited agreement paper -- has NO ablation on the number of CODE candidates at all. Only three sources touch k<=10: DOCE's Figure 3 (figure-only, CodeLlama-7B, HumanEval+ Filter ~65 -> Filter+MBR ~68 at n=5 and ~68 -> ~71 at n=10; MBPP-S+ ~72 -> ~73 and ~73 -> ~75), i.e. the increment of agreement over filtering collapses from +4.5/+12.0 at n=50 to +1 to +3 at n=5-10; Scaling Agentic Verifier at Best@8, where untrained random-input generation plus execution agreement gains +4.5 to +6.9 and beats trained CodeRM on 4 of 5 benchmarks; and Oracle Gap and Signal Fidelity (arXiv:2607.17531) at k=5, where a public-test verifier captures 69% of recoverable mass at 0% harm, a generated-test verifier only 23% (MCC 0.248, 35.77% coverage), and an LLM selector gains +3.50pp while HARMING 4.69% of already-correct answers. Nobody has published execution-agreement selection at k<=8 for a sub-8B quantized model on MBPP+HumanEval. That is our experiment, and it is a genuine hole. (4) The one result that endangers our null is ICSE 2026's SLM-as-a-judge (arXiv:2602.11911): at k=10 with 1.3B-4B generators, a FINE-TUNED 3B judge lifts Qwen2.5-Coder-3B from 0.377 random to 0.521 (+14.4). It requires supervised correctness labels on the same task distribution (which our design forbids and our budget cannot buy) and reports NO execution-agreement or visible-filter baseline -- its random floor of 0.377 sits far below our filtering baseline of 0.7455 -- but it forces us to narrow our claim from "no cheap learned selector works" to the claim we actually measured: "a cross-fitted learned selector over cheap STATIC features recovers none of the gap." (5) THE SINGLE BIGGEST THREAT TO TRANSFERRING DOCE'S 73-83% TO US, and it must be pre-registered: DOCE's MBR-Exec executes candidates on ALL evaluation unit-test INPUTS ("we use all unit tests given but only their inputs"), and DOCE reports that 80% of its trial tests overlap the evaluation tests. Under our strict split we have exactly ONE visible MBPP assertion, so we must SYNTHESISE the common inputs ourselves. CodeRM's table quantifies what pure candidate-vs-candidate agreement is worth without that privileged input set: MBR-Exec gains only +0.80 on MBPP+ versus +6.72 on HumanEval+ at N=100 with an 8B policy, because MBPP outputs are short and low-entropy so clusters barely discriminate. CodeT's AlphaCode-C row says the same thing from the other side: pure clustering is 3.5 to 10.7 points below clustering plus generated tests on identical pools. CONCRETE RECOMMENDATION. Run the k=8 execution-agreement arm, but run it in the CodeT/Semantic-Voting form, not the pure-clustering form: synthesise ~10 inputs per task (CodeT shows 10 tests already buy +4.3 to +9.5; Semantic Voting's 10 sketches x 5 instantiations is the recipe), cluster on executed behaviour rather than output text (worth 19-52pp per Semantic Voting), and always apply visible-assertion filtering FIRST since that is the highest-fidelity, zero-harm signal in every paper that measures it. Pre-register three arms against our 0.7455 filter baseline: execution agreement, lexical agreement (UCS, arXiv:2307.06857: +5.8 MBPP / +13.3 HumanEval over random at zero marginal cost -- if execution agreement cannot beat UCS, the execution machinery is not earning its compute), and visible-filter alone. Cost, INFERRED from our own numbers: 8 draws x 561 tasks x 2 receivers = 8,976 calls, ~9.9 hours at 909 calls/hour, plus ~1,122 input-synthesis calls (~1.2 h) -- about 11 hours total, comfortably inside budget and nowhere near the 123,000 calls (~135 h) that a LEVER-style k=100 trained verifier would need. Power, INFERRED: a +0.025 paired effect on 561 tasks with ~9% discordance gives SE ~0.013 and a 95% CI of roughly [0.000, 0.050] -- borderline, so put the statistical weight on the 3B receiver (gap 0.0737, expected effect 0.03-0.04, z ~2.4-3.1) and analyse the full audited pool rather than only the 230-task band. Report HARM RATE (already-correct answers broken by selection) as a first-class outcome, as arXiv:2607.17531 does; it is the metric our current audit is missing and the one that killed the LLM-selector arm in that paper. Finally, expect and pre-register an asymmetry: HumanEval will show little recoverable mass on the 7B (AceCoder's RM went negative there; 2607.17531 found only 4-6 of 164 recoverable at k=5 and refused to use HumanEval+ as its code benchmark), so the 3B receiver and the MBPP half are where our evidence will come from. If execution agreement underperforms, the cheapest documented next step is ACES-style leave-one-out-AUC test weighting (arXiv:2604.03922) -- pure post-processing on the execution matrix we will already have, at zero extra receiver calls.

DIRECT ANSWER IN THE REQUESTED FORM, with the honest caveat that no paper reports it in our cell. The single best-matched published number: execution-agreement clustering (functional majority vote) closes 57.5% of the oracle selection gap at k=64 on LiveCodeBench-v6 for Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 -- INFERRED by us from MEASURED-IN-PAPER values mean@64 = 30.8, FMV = 41.2, best@64 = 48.9 (arXiv:2604.15618). Supporting anchors: for frontier models on HumanEval+/MBPP+ at N=50, execution-grounded consensus drives residual SELECTION failure down to 1.5-2.7% while generation failure is 2.8-3.9%, i.e. it nearly closes the gap, and it beats output-pattern majority voting by 18-52 percentage points (arXiv:2605.08680, MEASURED-IN-PAPER). For a Qwen2.5-Coder-3B at N=16 on LiveCodeBench-v2, plain majority vote lifts 18.4 -> 25.2 and the 7B 29.4 -> 40.5 (arXiv:2502.14382, MEASURED-IN-PAPER), so agreement is not dead on small coder models -- but that same paper's ablation finds agreement against self-generated tests adds NOTHING over plain public-test filtering (53.1 vs 53.8 average; identical 42.3 for the 7B), and only inputs synthesised to DISTINGUISH candidates help (+3.7).  WHERE THE EVIDENCE STOPS, stated explicitly because it is the decision. (1) NOT A SINGLE PAPER FOUND reports execution-agreement selection on MBPP or HumanEval at k<=8 with a sub-8B quantized receiver. The closest are N=50 frontier models and an unquantized 4B at N=64. (2) Not a single stopping rule in this angle is validated on code at k<=8: ESC is the only one with MBPP numbers (L=10, w=5: SC 61.96 vs ESC 61.96 at 5.62 of 10 draws, MEASURED-IN-PAPER), MARS explicitly states code applicability remains to be validated, and DeepConf needs a 16-trace warmup that is twice our whole budget. (3) The only sub-8B quantized receiver anywhere in this literature is TrACE (arXiv:2604.08369), which runs Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct Q4_K_M on CPU at k_max 4 and 8 and saves 33.0% / 55.5% of calls at exactly 0.000 accuracy change -- but on n=50 GSM8K, single seed, CIs of width 0.21, no code, no oracle accounting. The k<=8 x sub-8B x code x execution-agreement cell is empty.  RECONCILED AGAINST OUR NUMBERS. Our 3B gap is 0.0737 and our visible-assertion adaptive rule already banks (0.7455-0.7169)/0.0737 = 38.8% of it for free (INFERRED). So agreement clustering must clear 38.8% merely to tie what we have, and the entire remaining head-room is 0.8192-0.7455 = 0.0451 absolute (INFERRED). If the 57.5% figure transferred exactly it would yield 0.575 x 0.0737 = 0.0424, i.e. +0.0138 over our current rule (INFERRED) -- a real but small effect. Three reasons it will transfer at less than face value: their gap is 18.1 points against our 7.4, so there is 2.5x less signal; their k is 64 against our 8, and with 8 draws a fragmented execution-signature space can leave the largest cluster at size 2, a coin flip; and for a receiver of our class agreement is measurably uninformative about correctness -- on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct the highest-agreement bin is correct only 52.5% of the time, on Llama-3-8B only 28.6% (lower than its own low-agreement bin), with entropy AUC 0.523-0.631, and majority voting HURTS per-problem accuracy on 56.6% / 65.7% of problems (arXiv:2608.11403, MEASURED-IN-PAPER). That is the same phenomenon as our own cheap-feature nulls (-0.18, -0.06, 0.00, 0.00, all intervals covering zero). On the 7B receiver the whole gap is 0.0351, so even a 57.5% recovery is +0.0202 and we should not expect to resolve it -- the 3B is the only receiver with enough gap to measure.  ON STOPPING SPECIFICALLY, the literature converges hard and the convergence is the finding: an optimal or near-optimal stop saves roughly a third of the draws and gains NO accuracy. Pandora's-Box/Weitzman UCB stopping, 15-35% fewer generations at equal quality (arXiv:2510.01394); ESC on MBPP, 43.8% fewer at L=10 (INFERRED from 5.62 of 10); TrACE on a quantized 3B, 33-56% fewer at exactly equal accuracy; MARS, 25-47% token savings; DeepConf, 43-84.7%. Every one of these is a COST result. This exactly matches our own audit, where adaptive best-of-N beat a real multi-turn feedback loop at lower cost (paired difference -0.0182, 95% CI [-0.0260,-0.0105]). Conclusion: do not frame stopping as a route to recovering the selection gap -- it is not, in any paper found.  IS THE STOPPING RULE EVER THE LEARNED OBJECT WITH A GUARANTEE? Yes, four ways, and the answer to 'should we learn it' is no. Formal guarantees exist: MARS gives P(early answer != full-budget answer) <= delta (Corollary 2.5); Bayesian optimal stopping proves asymptotic optimality with E[n*]/log(1/delta) -> 1/((p1-p2) log(p1/p2)) (ICML 2026, arXiv:2602.05395 Theorem 3.2); the bandit allocation paper proves total budget Theta-tilde(sum_x 1/Delta_x) versus Omega-tilde(max|S|/Delta_x) for uniform (arXiv:2506.12721 Theorem 1); and CITE gives anytime-valid false-certification control under ARBITRARY data-dependent stopping via e-processes (arXiv:2605.05873) -- that last one is the tool we should adopt, because our own stopping rule is data-dependent and fixed-n intervals are not valid for it. But on whether LEARNING the stopping rule pays: a cost-aware study finds the learned stopper beats the best simple scalar rule by only +0.028 [+0.002,+0.053] on GSM8K-32B and +0.023 [+0.005,+0.042] on MATH-500-8B, and LOSES on AIME-90 (-0.024, -0.010), MMLU-Pro and GPQA, with probe overhead shrinking 54.4% token savings to 32.5% and making black-box accounting uneconomical (arXiv:2606.30852, MEASURED-IN-PAPER). Independent corroboration of our own null.  THE ONE POSITIVE RESULT IN OUR BUDGET REGIME is allocation, not selection and not stopping: difficulty-aware bandit allocation gains +11.10 points on MATH-500 with Llama-3.1-8B AT BUDGET 8, +10.82 on AIME25 with Qwen3-4B, +11.23 on LiveCodeBench with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, at 1.82x-4.00x efficiency over uniform, with sub-8B models and budgets swept down to 1 (arXiv:2506.12721, MEASURED-IN-PAPER). Caveat we must not fudge: most of that gain is from not wasting draws on already-solved and hopeless tasks, and our 230-task informative band has already banked part of it -- the honest comparison is allocation WITHIN the band.  RECOMMENDED DECISION. Proceed, but reorder and gate. Step 0, zero new compute: compute the execution-signature cluster-size distribution and the top-two cluster margin p1-p2 on the existing 3-4 draw logs. This is the go/no-go. Both the ESC LLaMA-2-7B rows (agreement condition barely ever fires on a weak model: 8.99 of 10 draws spent on GSM8K, 9.67 of 10 on Last Letters) and the Bayesian stopping rate constant 1/((p1-p2) log(p1/p2)) (which diverges as p1 -> p2) predict that a weak receiver's clusters are too fragmented for either agreement-selection or agreement-stopping to bind at k=8. If the largest cluster is typically size 2 of 8 and p1-p2 is near zero, the answer to the viability question is NO and it costs nothing to learn that. If clusters are informative, run the k=8 design: 8 draws x 561 tasks = 4,488 receiver calls = 4.9 contended hours per receiver, 9.9 hours for both at 909 calls/hour (INFERRED) -- affordable, unlike the 20,000-call / 22-hour experiment. Design constraints the literature dictates: cluster on EXECUTION OUTPUTS, never on code strings (18-52 pp difference); synthesise inputs chosen to DISTINGUISH candidates rather than using arbitrary common inputs (+3.7 vs flat); do NOT spend compute comparing aggregation rules, since MBR-Exec, weighted voting and SemanticVote are statistically indistinguishable across 18 configurations (p>0.05, within 1.4 pp); probe inputs saturate by D=30 and D=5 is within 1.9 pp, so cap them cheaply; report the PAIRED per-task distribution and not just the mean, because aggregate gains hide per-problem harm on 56.6-65.7% of problems; use an e-process for the intervals because the stopping is data-dependent; and benchmark the honest baseline, which is our existing 0.7455 visible-assertion rule, not the 0.7169 single attempt. Pre-register the primary endpoint on the 3B only.

HEADLINE, in the requested form: execution-agreement clustering closes 14.0% of the oracle gap at k=8 on MBPP+/HumanEval+ for frozen sub-2B code models (8 of 57 available tasks pooled across six model-benchmark cells, ZERO of six significant, all p>=0.25) -- İşcan, arXiv:2606.16999, Table 1, MEASURED-IN-PAPER, with the fraction INFERRED by me. That is the only measurement in the literature taken at our k, against our exact baseline, with a hidden-test oracle, and it is a null.

THE FOUR CORROBORATING NUMBERS, all pointing the same way:
1. S* (arXiv:2502.14382, Findings EMNLP 2025) Table 3, N=8, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct: Public-test filtering alone 42.3; adding generated tests 42.3; adding an LLM judge 42.3. Three cheap selectors, ZERO recovery, on our model family at our k. Only GPT-4o-mini-driven adaptive input synthesis moved it, to 44.5 (+2.2pp).
2. CodeT (arXiv:2207.10397, ICLR 2023) Table 1: AlphaCode-C -- pure largest-output-cluster, verbatim our proposal -- recovers only 4.2-18.0% of the pass@100 gap and 10.9-29.3% of the pass@10 gap WITH a 100-sample pool, and goes NEGATIVE on CodeGen-Mono-16B on both benchmarks (INFERRED from MEASURED-IN-PAPER values). The weakest open model (InCoder-6B) is the worst cell: 10.9% of the k=10 HumanEval gap.
3. Semantic Voting (arXiv:2605.08680, May 2026) Table 4: on MBPP+ at N=50, execution clustering averages 0.32pp WORSE than 'return the first syntactically valid candidate' (93.36 vs 93.68), i.e. -13% of the BoN-to-oracle headroom; and SV, weighted voting and MBR-Exec are statistically indistinguishable on all 18 configurations.
4. İşcan's 'capability scissors' independently replicates our own audit: on 255 visible-passing candidates from Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B, a learned probe scores AUC 0.479 for HIDDEN correctness while the same features hit AUC 0.985 for visible-pass. That is our GBM/logistic null (fractions -0.18, -0.06, 0.00, 0.00) reproduced with different features on a different model family. Our null was not a modelling failure.

WHAT THIS CONCLUDES ABOUT RECOVERABILITY. Applied to our numbers, the most favourable defensible transfer rate (21%, CodeT's AlphaCode-C on MBPP with 100 draws -- an upper bound, since we have 8) predicts 0.0155 on the 3B, about 7 tasks of 448, and 0.0074 on the 7B, about 3 tasks. The İşcan rate (14%, measured at k=8) predicts 0.0103 and 0.0049 -- 5 and 2 tasks. Both sit inside the interval widths our own audits already produce, so a 20,000-call / 22-contended-hour experiment on this arm is powered to produce another interval covering zero. İşcan's Proposition 1 sharpens this: a distribution-free do-no-harm certificate cannot bound population harm at 5% even at ZERO observed harm unless n>=45, so our 230-task informative band can support a do-no-harm claim but not a small positive effect.

THE MECHANISM, WHICH IS WHY THIS IS STRUCTURAL AND NOT A TUNING PROBLEM. A leakage-free selector can only net-gain on a 'consensus trap' task: the visible-passing majority is hidden-WRONG and a hidden-correct candidate is also in the pool. İşcan measures that mass as near zero (the triggering bug appeared on 0/10 and 2/16 tasks on purpose-built trap benchmarks, never as the consensus majority; ~83% of real bugs are invisible to any sound metamorphic relation). And at k=8 clustering is close to vacuous by construction: Semantic Voting MEASURES 1.2-1.5 clusters per problem at N=50 with the largest holding 38-48 of 50, so at k=8 the modal outcome is one cluster containing everything, making largest-cluster selection identical to our existing 0.7455 baseline. AlphaCode -- the origin of the method -- needed ~100,000 draws per problem with >99% filtered out, and its Figure 3D shows the clustering benefit GROWING in k, i.e. smallest exactly where we sit.

THE HONEST DAYLIGHT, and it is narrow but real. (a) NOBODY has ever run this on a QUANTIZED model; every sub-8B cell in the literature is full precision, and q4_k_m could plausibly change the error-correlation structure clustering depends on -- direction unknown. (b) İşcan's models are 0.5-1.5B with headroom of 4.27-4.59pp; our 3B gap is 7.37pp, 60-70% larger, so our trap mass may genuinely be bigger. (c) İşcan's own predicted boundary condition is ours: 'a WEAKER visible-test filter (so that visible-passing, hidden-wrong majorities become common) would refill the consensus trap.' Our strict one-assertion-visible MBPP split IS that weaker filter. But note this is his PREDICTION, not his measurement -- and the one paper that did measure the example-assertion-only input condition (Semantic Voting Table 1) found it the WORST of four input strategies, costing 6-11.3pp, while CodeT Appendix B found that leaving example assertions in the context makes its pass@1 NEGATIVE by up to -4.2%.

RECOMMENDED DECISION. Do not spend 22 contended hours on execution-agreement as a confirmatory arm; the prior is a null and the design is underpowered for the effect size the literature supports. Instead spend under an hour on the kill-switch that nobody has published: count the execution-fingerprint CLUSTER DISTRIBUTION at k=3-4 on the existing logs, and count consensus-trap tasks directly (visible-passing majority hidden-wrong AND a hidden-correct candidate present). If trap mass is near zero on our own pool, the arm is dead on our own data, at zero compute cost, and that measurement is itself publishable as a quantized-receiver replication of İşcan's negative. Then move the project's weight onto STOPPING, where the evidence is positive and consistent: agreement-based early stopping buys ~19% compute saving at a zero-harm operating point (İşcan's ACE, Hoeffding-Bentkus Learn-then-Test) and ~16% in the newest work (CoTT, arXiv:2609.12489, $0.065 vs $0.077, and note its UNGATED variant actually scored higher on HumanEval-R+ Top-1). Two independent 2026 papers converging on 'execution agreement is worth a 16-19% compute saving and approximately zero accuracy' is the most reliable regularity in this search, and it dovetails with our own strongest measured result -- adaptive best-of-N beating a real multi-turn feedback loop at lower cost, -0.0182 [-0.0260, -0.0105]. That is a compute-efficiency and stopping-rule paper with a known-positive effect, not a selection-accuracy paper fighting a measured null.

RECOVERABLE, BUT ONLY BARELY, AND NOT BY MODEL-WRITTEN TESTS. Split the untested candidate in two, because the literature treats them very differently.

(A) Model-generated tests with expected OUTPUTS: drop this arm. Three independent measurements condemn it at our scale. At N=8 with a Qwen2.5-Coder-7B receiver, generated tests scored 42.3 versus 42.3 for the public/visible test alone -- exactly zero gain -- and averaged across four models they were NET NEGATIVE, 53.1 versus 53.8 (arXiv:2502.14382, MEASURED). A sub-8B test writer gets 4 in 10 individual tests wrong: Llama3.1-8B accuracy 60.02%, FAR 13.66%, FRR 46.13% on HumanEval Plus, and aggregating 100 tests makes FAR WORSE, 13.66% -> 20.44% (arXiv:2501.01054, MEASURED). With only 8 draws, a 46% false-reject rate will routinely discard the one correct candidate, which is the mechanism that produced our own negative recovered fractions of -0.18 and -0.06. And the result would be uninterpretable anyway: test generation is inflated by 31.88 percentage points (pass@5 44.45% vs 12.57%) on pre-leaked versus unleaked functions (arXiv:2508.00408, MEASURED), and MBPP/HumanEval are the pre-leaked class. Worse, the predictable failure mode is trivial -- a 3B asked for MBPP tests will largely regurgitate the single visible assertion, making the selector definitionally identical to the 0.7455 baseline we already have. CodeT itself stripped docstring examples for exactly this reason (arXiv:2207.10397, MEASURED).

(B) Cross-candidate execution AGREEMENT over generated probe INPUTS (no expected outputs): this is the right experiment, it is leakage-immune by construction, and it is cheap -- but expect 0 to 2 points, not 7. The pro case: on top of a pass-filter, MBR-Exec recovers 63% of the residual oracle gap on HumanEval+ (70.1 from 59.7, oracle 76.2) and 76% on MBPP-S+ (69.3 from 60.8, oracle 72.0) for CodeLlama-7B-Instruct (arXiv:2408.13745, INFERRED from measured cells); output-consensus clustering as a tie-break adds +8.8pp average BoN for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (arXiv:2605.23491, MEASURED). The deflations: DOCE's probe inputs are the benchmark's REAL evaluation test inputs, which our visible/hidden split forbids, and its filter needs real expected outputs -- so 63-76% is the ceiling under perfect probes, not our expected value. At N=8 the honest same-scale number is +2.2pp for a 7B (42.3 -> 44.5, adaptive distinguishing inputs, arXiv:2502.14382, MEASURED), and that method needs the model to referee two outputs, which a q4_k_m 3B does poorly. Scaling: +2.2pp is ~30% of our 3B's 7.37pp gap and would overshoot the 7B's 3.51pp. At the origin of the method, DeepMind bought only +2.6pp from clustering with 50 probe inputs and 100,000 candidates (arXiv:2203.07814, MEASURED) -- the same order as our entire 7B gap.

THE NEAR-SCOOP, AND THE STRONGEST SINGLE DATUM: arXiv:2606.16999 already ran our experiment -- k=8, frozen small code models (0.5B-1.5B), HumanEval+/MBPP+, consensus selectors including MBR-Exec -- and found them "null (ties BoN)", net <= +3 tasks, NEVER significant (p >= 0.25), against headroom of 11-17 of 370 tasks on MBPP+ (3.0-4.6pp INFERRED) and 0-7 of 164 on HumanEval+. It independently reproduces our cheap-selector null and extends it to the exact method we were about to test. It is an unreviewed single-author preprint, so treat it as a strong prior, not a verdict -- but plan as if agreement clustering will also come out null. Its two POSITIVE results are the ones to steal: (i) a fallback that fires only when NO candidate passes the visible assertion, worth +12 tasks on HumanEval+ and +33 on MBPP+ for DeepSeek-1.3B (p = 2.4e-4 and 1.2e-10) -- this maps exactly onto our 0.7169 -> 0.7455 visible-filter step; (ii) adaptive consensus EARLY STOP with a distribution-free do-no-harm certificate, 19.1% compute saving at zero measured harm (p = 0.0165).

WHERE THE EVIDENCE IS SILENT, AND IT MATTERS: nobody reports fraction-of-oracle-gap recovered by agreement clustering at k<=8 for a 3B-class model on MBPP/HumanEval with a strict hidden-test split. Nobody has measured FAR/FRR for test generation below 8B. Nobody has measured any of this under quantization. Most published selection work runs k = 50 to 1000 (CodeT n=100 with ~500 assertions; B4 100+100; ACES ~200 candidates and ~500 tests; Semantic Voting N=50; AlphaCode 8,192-100,000), and the frontier-model results (SemanticVote at 91-99% pass@1) are saturated and non-transferable. Our k<=8, sub-8B, quantized regime is genuinely unmeasured -- which is the one good reason to proceed.

WHAT TO DO, RECONCILED AGAINST OUR NUMBERS AND 909 CALLS/HOUR. Three cheap arms, all together well under one contended hour of receiver time, versus the 22 hours a 20,000-call test-generation study would cost. (1) Probe-input agreement, tie-break only, layered on the visible-assertion filter: ask for INPUTS only, never expected outputs; use LLM seeds plus free type-aware Python mutation (arXiv:2305.01210); 5-20 probe inputs suffices per DOCE (peak at 5 on MBPP-S+, 20 on HumanEval+), Semantic Voting (saturates past D=30, D=5 already near-peak) and AlphaCode (50) -- so ~230-500 receiver calls for seeds, executions free. Prefer behavioural-class sketches over raw fuzzing or the docstring example: input STRATEGY is worth up to 11.3pp while the AGGREGATOR choice is worth only +/-1.2pp (SemanticVote vs MBR-Exec), so put the effort in input generation, not in the voting rule. Sample hotter than default -- DOCE found T ~ 1.6-1.8 optimal for HumanEval/MBPP-class tasks. (2) A small-model-as-judge control arm, because arXiv:2602.11911 (ICSE'26) is the only paper matching us on BOTH axes and shows Qwen2.5-Coder 3B going 0.361 -> 0.443 -> 0.495 -> 0.521 at k = 1, 2, 5, 10, beating random by +0.144 at k=10 while log-likelihood (our closest analogue, 0.397 vs random 0.377) gives nearly nothing. If the judge works at 3B and clustering does not, that is the paper; its absence is the first question a reviewer asks. (3) Make STOPPING the headline, not selection. Our own adaptive best-of-N already beat a multi-turn loop at lower cost (-0.0182, CI [-0.0260,-0.0105]); arXiv:2606.16999 certifies 19.1% compute savings at zero harm; and arXiv:2411.17501 proves why accuracy-gain claims are bounded for weak models with imperfect verifiers -- the false-positive rate of any selector we can build cannot be resampled away, and weak models are measured to have the highest such rates on HumanEval/MBPP. Stopping is where the bound does not bite, because it is evaluated as compute saved at fixed accuracy. POWER WARNING: expect an effect of 1-3 points against gaps of 3.51 and 7.37 points; power the design for a couple of points on the 230-task informative band, and expect intervals that cover zero on the 7B. Add B4 (arXiv:2409.08692) as the reference selector if any pass-matrix arm is run -- it is closed-form over a matrix we already have and costs zero extra calls.
